instruction.text: Match the syntactical devices to their description.

atoms.a: a list of words that are thematically related and share a similar meaning
a comparison between two pairs of relationships that highlights their similarities
a repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive sentences or lines
a sentence that runs over from one line to the next without punctuation
a list of things that refer to a shared broader topic
similar grammatical structures in successive phrases
the repeated usage of the same words or phrases
She felt overwhelmed, exhausted, defeated, broken, and utterly alone.
The crowd surged forward, pushing, shoving, trampling, clawing their way toward the stage.

The day is gone, and the darkness Falls from the wings of Night, As a feather is wafted downward From an eagle in his flight.

(Longfellow, The Day is Done, lines 1-4)
Reading literature is like peeling an onion. Each layer you remove reveals deeper complexity.
At dawn the mist clings to the fields, At dawn the birds test their first notes, At dawn the world remembers how to begin again.

Every day, every night, in every way, I am getting better and better.

(Émile Coué)

I think that I shall never see
A poem lovely as a tree.

(Kilmer, Trees, lines 1-2)

We slowly drove — He knew no haste
And I had put away
My labor and my leisure too,
For His Civility —

(Dickinson, Because I could not stop for Death, lines 5-8)
The ensemble featured a trumpet, saxophone, piano, bass, and drums.

Roses are red, violets are blue, sugar is sweet, and so are you.

(Traditional rhyme)

Who is here so base that would be a bondman? [...]
Who is here so rude that would not be a Roman? [...]
Who is here so vile that will not love his country?

(Shakespeare, Julius Caesar, 3.2.29-33)

I’ll give my jewels for a set of beads, My gorgeous palace for a hermitage, My gay apparel for an almsman’s gown, My figured goblets for a dish of wood, My scepter for a palmer’s walking-staff,
[...]

(Shakespeare, Richard II, 3.3.152-156)

Tomorrow and tomorrow and tomorrow

(Shakespeare, Macbeth, 5.5.22)

My kingdom for a horse! My kingdom for a horse!

(Shakespeare, Richard III, 5.4.13)
